chunks: Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah from Abu Ja'far, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fudaylah ibn Ayyub, from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi 'Abdillah, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who deliberately broke his fast for one day in the month of Ramadan. He said: 'Upon him is fifteen sa' for each poor person, a mud with the mud of the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) is better.'

And from him, from Abu Ja'far, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from al-Mashriqi, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about a man who deliberately broke his fast for days in Ramadan, what is the expiation upon him? He wrote (replying): 'Whoever deliberately breaks his fast for one day in Ramadan, upon him is freeing a believing slave, and he fasts one day in place of one day.'

And there is no contradiction in these narrations, because what is obligatory upon the one who breaks his fast deliberately for one day is one of the three things: freeing a slave, or feeding sixty poor people, or fasting two consecutive months. Whichever of the three he does, it suffices him. So whenever he is unable to do one of them, he fasts what he is able to do and gives charity with what he can, and this is with the varying conditions of people from weakness and strength.
And it has been said that he fasts eighteen days in place of freeing the slave and feeding (the poor). That which indicates this is what he narrated:

key_terms.صَاع: A traditional unit of volume for measuring food
key_terms.كَفَّارَة: Expiation or compensation for a religious violation
key_terms.مُد: A smaller unit of volume, typically half a sa'

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for deliberately breaking a fast in Ramadan according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* outlines the three alternative expiations (kaffarah) for deliberately breaking a Ramadan fast: freeing a slave, feeding sixty poor, or fasting two consecutive months. It clarifies that these are mutually exclusive options where performing any one suffices, with flexibility for those unable to meet the primary requirement. The text also records a secondary scholarly opinion that fasting eighteen days can serve as a substitute for both freeing a slave and feeding the poor, reflecting the practical adaptability in Shia jurisprudence.
